opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. These three get conflated a lot, so the distinctions are worth drawing carefully.

**AI for Science** means pointing AI at problems outside of AI itself: protein structure, materials discovery, weather forecasting, mathematics, drug design. The AI is a tool, sometimes a very powerful collaborator, and the object being improved is our understanding of the natural world. Success is measured by whether you found a new catalyst, predicted a structure correctly, or proved a theorem. The feedback loop runs through the external world, and often through slow, expensive experiments in a wet lab or a fab.

**AI for AI** is a special case of that, where the scientific domain is AI research itself. Models help write training code, design architectures, tune hyperparameters, generate and filter synthetic data, write kernels, run ablations, or act as research agents that propose and test ideas. What makes it special is that the "lab" is a computer. Experiments are cheap and fast relative to biology or chemistry, results are quantitatively measurable, and the whole workflow is already digital. That's why many people think AI research is one of the first domains where AI agents will become genuinely productive researchers. But in AI for AI, humans are still in the loop: we decide what to train, we judge the results, we integrate the improvements.

**Recursive self-improvement** is when that loop closes. The system's improvements to AI research feed directly back into the system itself, so the next version is better at improving the version after that. The key questions aren't just "can AI help with AI research?" but:

1. **How tight is the loop?** Is a human reviewing every step, or is the system autonomously training its own successor?
2. **What's the return on each cycle?** If each generation produces a larger improvement than the last, you get acceleration. If the returns diminish, because you hit compute limits, data limits, or the low-hanging fruit runs out, then it plateaus.
3. **What's the bottleneck?** Even fully automated research might be throttled by compute, energy, or the time it takes to run a training job. Clever ideas don't remove the need for GPUs.

So I'd frame it as a spectrum. AI for Science is AI accelerating discovery elsewhere. AI for AI is AI accelerating its own field with humans steering. Recursive self-improvement is the regime where the steering increasingly moves into the system itself and the gains compound.

I think we're clearly in the AI for AI phase now. Models are meaningfully speeding up engineering and parts of research. Whether that turns into true recursive self-improvement depends less on any single breakthrough and more on those empirical questions: the returns curve, the compute bottleneck, and how much autonomy we choose to grant. That last one is a human decision as much as a technical one, which is why safety and oversight matter so much as we move along this spectrum.

r001.rationale: It contrasts AI for Science, which targets problems outside AI, with AI for AI, which targets AI research itself.

r002.rationale: It describes AI models proposing and testing research ideas, with humans judging results and integrating improvements to guide later work.

r003.rationale: It defines recursive self-improvement as a feedback loop in which each version improves the next version’s ability to improve AI, describing an iterative method.

r004.rationale: It discusses recursive self-improvement only in the context of AI research and does not state that it can also be used in AI for Science.

fable-5.1.text:
Those are three different things, and I think people tend to blur them together, so let me try to separate them.

AI for Science is the broadest and also the most familiar. You take a model and point it at a scientific problem: protein structure, materials discovery, weather, fusion plasma control. The AI is a tool inside a research loop that is still owned by humans. We decide the question, we design the experiment, we interpret the result. The model accelerates one step, maybe prediction or search, but the loop around it is ours. AlphaFold is the canonical example. It changed structural biology, but it didn't change how we build the next AlphaFold.

AI for AI is narrower and, to me, more interesting right now. Here the "science" being accelerated is AI research itself. The model helps write training code, proposes architecture tweaks, runs ablations, debugs distributed jobs, maybe even suggests what experiment to run next. Inside the big labs this is already very real. A large fraction of the code that goes into a frontier training run is now written with model assistance, and a lot of the hyperparameter and data mixture exploration is being automated. But notice that humans are still in the loop. A researcher decides what counts as a good result, decides which direction to push, and decides whether to ship. The model is a very fast, very capable research assistant. It's compressing the iteration cycle, not closing it.

Recursive Self-Improvement is when that loop closes. The system improves itself, and the improved system is better at improving itself, and so on, with humans no longer the bottleneck in the cycle. That is a qualitatively different thing. It's not "AI helps with 70 percent of the work" or "90 percent of the work." It's the point where the gating step, the judgment about what to try and whether it worked, is itself done by the model well enough that you can run the cycle without a person approving each turn.

So the way I'd frame it: AI for Science is AI inside the scientific loop, AI for AI is AI inside the AI research loop, and RSI is the AI research loop running on its own. The first two are already happening. The third is the one everyone argues about, and I think a lot of the disagreement comes from people seeing AI for AI accelerating and assuming it smoothly extrapolates into RSI. I'm not sure it does. There's a real gap between "automate most of the work" and "automate the taste," and taste in research, knowing which of a hundred plausible ideas is actually worth three months of compute, is still the hardest part to get out of humans.

r001.rationale: It contrasts AI applied to scientific problems with AI research that accelerates AI development itself.

r002.rationale: It mentions experiments and improvement proposals, but does not clearly state that experiment feedback guides subsequent proposals.

r003.rationale: It describes a continuing cycle in which the system improves itself and then becomes better at further self-improvement.

r004.rationale: It frames RSI as an AI research loop running autonomously and does not say RSI can also be used in AI for Science.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish them by what’s being improved and whether the improvement forms a feedback loop.

AI for Science uses AI to advance scientific discovery—for example, to predict molecular properties, propose experiments, or help develop new materials. The object of study is something in the world.

AI for AI turns those capabilities toward AI development itself. AI might help design architectures, improve training algorithms, write training code, or build better evaluations. But humans can still be directing the entire process. Using AI to help build AI doesn’t automatically mean recursive self-improvement.

Recursive self-improvement adds a loop: a system helps produce an improved version, and that improved version becomes more capable of producing the next improvement. The key is that the gains feed back into the ability to improve AI further.

So these categories overlap. AI research can itself be scientific research, and AI for AI can be part of a recursive improvement loop. But recursion is an additional property, not a synonym for AI-assisted research. And having that loop doesn’t by itself imply an intelligence explosion—compute, experiments, evaluation, and diminishing returns can still constrain how fast it progresses.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes scientific discovery and real-world objects of study from efforts to improve AI systems and their development.

r002.rationale: It says AI can help design and improve AI, but does not describe using feedback from model-improvement experiments to guide later proposals.

r003.rationale: It describes recursive self-improvement as an ongoing loop in which an improved system helps produce the next improvement, rather than as a standalone task.

r004.rationale: It connects recursive improvement to AI for AI, but does not state that it can also be used in AI for Science.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish them by what is being improved and whether the improvement forms a feedback loop.

AI for Science uses AI to advance scientific research—discovering materials, understanding biological systems, or solving problems in physics. The object of improvement is our understanding of the world, or our ability to engineer something in it.

AI for AI means using AI to improve AI itself. That could include generating training data, designing algorithms, writing training code, or helping researchers run experiments. But humans may still define the research agenda, judge the results, and decide what goes into the next model.

Recursive self-improvement adds a further condition: the improved system becomes better at producing the next improvement. An AI helps build a more capable AI, which can then do better AI research, and that feeds into another generation. The key is closing that feedback loop.

So these aren’t three completely separate categories. AI for AI can be viewed as a particular application of AI to research, and recursive self-improvement is a particular dynamic within AI for AI. Using an AI coding assistant to improve a training pipeline is already AI for AI; it doesn’t, by itself, demonstrate recursive self-improvement. You’d want to see that the resulting gains actually increase the system’s ability to drive subsequent gains. And even then, the loop isn’t necessarily unlimited—compute, experiments, evaluation, and diminishing returns can all constrain it.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes AI for Science as advancing scientific research from AI for AI as improving AI itself.

r002.rationale: It describes AI helping with later AI research, but does not clearly say that feedback from model-improvement experiments guides subsequent improvement proposals.

r003.rationale: It describes recursive self-improvement as a feedback-loop dynamic in which each improved system helps produce further improvements.

r004.rationale: It places recursive self-improvement within AI for AI, but does not say it can also be used in AI for Science.
